title: From Naperville to Nassau Hall: Indian American Jaisnav Rajesh Wins Princeton's Highest Campus Honor
excerpt: The Illinois-raised computer science senior, who researched at Fermilab and Peking University, is one of eight students to receive the 2026 Spirit of Princeton Award for transforming campus life.
body:
Every spring, Princeton University selects a handful of undergraduates whose contributions to campus life are so sweeping that they warrant a formal honour: the Allen Macy Dulles Spirit of Princeton Award. This year, one of the eight recipients is Jaisnav Rajesh, an Indian American computer science senior from Plainfield, Illinois — and his résumé reads less like a college student’s and more like a mid-career leader’s.

## A Campus Polymath

Rajesh was chosen from more than 200 nominations across the campus community. The breadth of his involvement is striking. He serves as a residential college adviser at New College West and sits on the residential college leadership team. He works as a peer career adviser at the Center for Career Development, helping fellow students navigate post-graduation paths. He is a community ambassador for the Scholars Institute Fellows Program, which supports first-generation and lower-income students — a role that reflects a personal commitment to making elite institutions more accessible.

Perhaps most notably, he manages the Princeton Financial Literacy Program, an initiative that teaches students the kind of practical money skills that Ivy League curricula rarely touch. Financial literacy is a recurring gap for first-generation college students, and for children of immigrants who grew up watching their parents navigate an unfamiliar financial system, the programme carries a particular resonance.

## From Fermilab to Peking University

Rajesh’s academic footprint extends well beyond Princeton’s campus. He has conducted technology policy research through Princeton’s China Lab, a programme under the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies, which included a stint at Peking University. He has also worked as a lead researcher at Fermilab, the US Department of Energy’s particle physics laboratory in Illinois, where he applied machine learning techniques to analyse bias in scientific data. His findings were presented at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) and the Harvard Science Research Conference — venues where most presenters hold doctoral degrees.

The combination of hard science research with policy work in Beijing is unusual and deliberate. At a moment when the US-China technology relationship shapes everything from semiconductor export controls to AI governance, a 22-year-old who can operate credibly in both worlds is exactly the kind of talent that think tanks, government agencies, and technology firms are competing for.

## The Diaspora Pattern

Rajesh’s story fits a pattern that readers of The Videshi will recognise: Indian American students disproportionately appearing at the top of academic and civic achievement rankings in the United States. Thirteen Indian American students were among the 40 finalists in this year’s Regeneron Science Talent Search. Eight won Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowships. Four were recently cleared for positions at Stanford.

The pattern is not accidental. It reflects a community-wide emphasis on education, a willingness to invest in extracurricular depth rather than breadth, and — less often discussed — a network of cultural expectations that pushes second-generation Indian Americans to treat college not as an endpoint but as a launchpad.

## What Comes Next

Rajesh, whose family roots trace to the Indian diaspora, grew up in Illinois and attended Waubonsie Valley High School in Naperville — a suburb that has become, along with similar enclaves in New Jersey, the Bay Area, and North Texas, a crucible for Indian American academic talent. His Spirit of Princeton Award follows an earlier honour: the A. James Fisher, Jr. Memorial Award in late 2025, recognising his entrepreneurial energy in expanding educational access and financial literacy for lower-income youth.

For NRI families watching from abroad, stories like Rajesh’s serve a dual function. They are a source of pride — a validation that the sacrifices of emigration are paying generational dividends. But they also raise a quieter question: what would a mind like this have accomplished in India, had the opportunities been comparable? The answer, increasingly, is that India is trying to find out. IITs and IISc are investing in undergraduate research programmes. The National Research Foundation is scaling up. Whether those efforts can compete with the Princeton-Fermilab-CERN pipeline that Rajesh navigated remains to be seen.

For now, the Spirit of Princeton Award belongs to Jaisnav Rajesh — a reminder that the Indian diaspora’s deepest investment is not in real estate or remittances, but in the next generation.
author: Diaspora Desk
